name: Evidence for Anomalous Lepton Production in e+ − e− Annihilation
notes: The paper title says "Evidence", so result_type is evidence; the tau was established as a lepton by later work (Perl Nobel lecture) and the 1995 Nobel Prize.
The SSRL history page says the tau was "discovered at SPEAR in 1976"; the paper is dated December 1975, used here.

summary.plain: In December 1975 the Mark I experiment at SLAC's SPEAR ring reported electron-muon events with no other particles that no known process could explain. The events came from pairs of a new, heavy charged lepton, later named the tau, the third charged lepton after the electron and muon.
summary.technical: Mark I: e⁺e⁻ → e^± + μ^∓ + missing energy with no other charged particles or photons, mostly at or above 4 GeV centre-of-mass energy; the missing-energy and momentum spectra require at least two additional particles per event; 'we have no conventional explanation'. The Mark I authors suggested a pair of new particles of mass 1.6-2.0 GeV/c²; the interpretation as a heavy lepton (τ) was established over the following two years.

title: Evidence for Anomalous Lepton Production in e+ − e− Annihilation
why_it_matters: Martin Perl shared the 1995 Nobel Prize in Physics for the discovery of the tau lepton; SLAC's history calls it the third charged lepton after the electron (1897) and the muon (1937).
